title: Sizing the ETF Opportunity: Active ETFs Move to Center Stage
summary: For analysts, nothing is more satisfying than raising long-term forecasts that had once seemed aggressive, if not unattainable. That’s where we find ourselves today with U.S. Exchange-Traded Funds’ assets under management. Citi Research explores U.S. ETFs’ more mature growth phase in this new Must C report.
body_text: Must C: Sizing the ETF Opportunity — Active ETFs Move to Center Stage Download Here A new Citi Research report from a team of strategists led by Drew Pettit explores how the growth of U.S. Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) has exceeded the team’s most optimistic expectations, with the main driver organic inflows and not just strong risk-asset returns. Given this reality, the team now revisits its forecasting framework in its new Must C report, updating its aggregate projections for U.S. ETF assets under management (AUM). A year ago, we laid out our roadmap to the next $10 trillion in U.S. ETF assets. Our core thesis was straightforward: ETFs would continue to take share from mutual funds as professional product innovation expanded access to more precisely engineered investment solutions. Central to that view was a slow burn battle for the core of asset allocation itself, where active approaches would begin to reclaim share from traditional index strategies. We saw this shift as driven by growing awareness of the idiosyncrasies embedded in concentrated and widely followed equity benchmarks, pushing investors toward more differentiated, outcome oriented solutions. In fixed income and other asset classes, the story was already unfolding — index approaches often overlooked or underweighted entire segments that offered distinct return streams. Active ETFs benefited directly from this gap, especially as liquidity ecosystems improved, democratized access, and, in some cases, created entirely new investable universes. In our early Must C research (see Sizing the ETF Opportunity: From Passive Revolution to Active Evolution ), we highlighted ETF encroachment on mutual funds, particularly outside of defined contribution channels. Importantly, we never viewed this as simply another wave of passive adoption. Instead, we saw the ETF wrapper becoming the preferred vehicle for active differentiation across asset classes, strategy design, and newly accessible corners of the global opportunity set. While those views were clearly bullish, the industry’s recent growth has exceeded even our most optimistic expectations, with this growth driven largely by organic inflows rather than just strong risk asset returns. Given this reality, we’re revisiting our forecasting framework and updating our aggregate U.S. ETF AUM projections. These are our current scenarios: Base case: $25 trillion in 2030, $42 trillion in 2035. Growth continues but naturally decelerates as the industry matures, with a more balanced mix of flows and returns. Bull case: $32 trillion in 2030, $73 trillion in 2035. Overall growth rates resemble the past decade, with organic flows remaining the dominant driver alongside strong market performance. Bear case: $20 trillion in 2030, $23 trillion in 2035. New forms of investment funds or investment technologies disrupt the ETF industry, much as ETFs disrupted mutual funds. Growth is largely a function of returns, offsetting outflows in later years — a scenario similar to what we see with mutual funds today. Recent annual U.S. ETF AUM have slightly exceeded our prior bull case. A modeling change reflects this: We now project flows as a percentage of beginning of year AUM rather than extrapolating monthly run rates, which better captures compounding effects in a larger industry. Historically, U.S. ETF AUM has grown at a remarkable 20% annualized pace, with roughly 60% coming from flows. In our base case, we assume meaningful deceleration in flow driven growth as the asset base expands, combined with some minor deceleration in returns. That produces a more even organic inorganic growth split. In the bull case, flows continue to outpace returns as the primary contributor, even while acknowledging ETFs are no longer an early stage industry. In the bear case, the setup increasingly resembles today’s mutual-fund complex, with returns often offsetting negative outflows. Over time, we expect flows as a percentage of AUM to naturally decelerate. Recent years surprised to the upside due to innovation across cryptocurrencies, collateralized loan obligations, and equity derivatives, aided by a more permissive ETF launch environment. When standardized by AUM, however, exponential dollar growth translates into a linear decline in flow intensity — exactly what we’d expect from a maturing industry. Our base case reflects the 10 year historical trend, excluding 2024 and 2025. On returns, aggregate U.S. ETF performance has closely mirrored a globally diversified 60/40 portfolio, averaging 7.3% annualized during the past decade. That serves as the anchor for our assumptions: 6% in our base case, 8% in our bull case, and 4% in our bear case. These sit comfortably within long run historical distributions and imply some modest conservatism amid today’s valuation and rate environment. Ultimately, our earlier forecasts proved conservative because flows, not markets, did the heavy lifting. By reframing growth in terms of flows relative to AUM, we arrive at higher — but we believe more realistic — long term estimates. To us, $25 trillion in U.S. ETF assets by the end of this decade looks clearly attainable, with more than $40 trillion plausible over the next 10 years as innovation continues within an increasingly mature industry. Non-GAAP Financial Measures Our reported results are presented in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (“GAAP”). We also disclose Funds From Operations (“FFO”), Adjusted Funds From Operations (“AFFO”), and Pro Forma Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (“Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA”), all of which are non-GAAP financial measures. We believe these non-GAAP financial measures are useful to investors because they are widely accepted industry measures used by analysts and investors to compare the operating performance of REITs. FFO, AFFO, and Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA do not represent cash generated from operating activities and are not necessarily indicative of cash available to fund cash requirements; accordingly, they should not be considered alternatives to net income or loss as a performance measure or cash flows from operations as reported on our statement of cash flows as a liquidity measure and should be considered in addition to, and not in lieu of, GAAP financial measures. We compute FFO in accordance with the definition adopted by the Board of Governors of the National Association of Real Estate Investment Trusts, or NAREIT. NAREIT defines FFO as GAAP net income or loss adjusted to exclude real estate related depreciation and amortization, as well as extraordinary items (as defined by GAAP) such as net gain or loss from sales of depreciable real estate assets, impairment write-downs associated with depreciable real estate assets and impairments associated with the implementation of current expected credit losses on commercial loans and investments at the time of origination, including the pro rata share of such adjustments of unconsolidated subsidiaries. To derive AFFO, we further modify the NAREIT computation of FFO to include other adjustments to GAAP net income related to non-cash revenues and expenses such as loss on extinguishment of debt, amortization of above- and below-market lease related intangibles, straight-line rental revenue, amortization of deferred financing costs, non-cash compensation, and other non-cash adjustments to income or expense. Such items may cause short-term fluctuations in net income or loss but have no impact on operating cash flows or long-term operating performance. We use AFFO as one measure of our performance when we formulate corporate goals. To derive Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA, GAAP net income or loss is adjusted to exclude extraordinary items (as defined by GAAP), net gain or loss from sales of depreciable real estate assets, impairment write-downs associated with depreciable real estate assets and impairments associated with the implementation of current expected credit losses on commercial loans and investments at the time of origination and/or payoff, and real estate related depreciation and amortization including the pro rata share of such adjustments of unconsolidated subsidiaries, non-cash revenues and expenses such as straight-line rental revenue, amortization of deferred financing costs, loss on extinguishment of debt, above- and below-market lease related intangibles, non-cash compensation, other non-cash income or expense, and other non-recurring items such as disposition management fees and commission fees. Cash interest expense is also excluded from Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA, and GAAP net income or loss is adjusted for the annualized impact of acquisitions, dispositions and other similar activities. FFO is used by management, investors and analysts to facilitate meaningful comparisons of operating performance between periods and among our peers primarily because it excludes the effect of real estate depreciation and amortization and net gains or losses on sales, which are based on historical costs and implicitly assume that the value of real estate diminishes predictably over time, rather than fluctuating based on existing market conditions. We believe that AFFO is an additional useful supplemental measure for investors to consider because it will help them to better assess our operating performance without the distortions created by other non-cash revenues or expenses. We also believe that Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA is an additional useful supplemental measure for investors to consider as it allows for a better assessment of our operating performance without the distortions created by other non-cash revenues, expenses or certain effects of the Company’s capital structure on our operating performance. FFO, AFFO, and Pro Forma Adjusted EBITDA may not be comparable to similarly titled measures employed by other companies. body_text: Red Cat’s Teal Drones subsidiary received a $2.49 million firm-fixed-price contract from the U.S. Air Force Security Forces Center for Black Widow unmanned aircraft, training, batteries, spares and related support. The systems will be used in a technical and operational assessment of Black Widow as a potential successor to the Air Force Security Forces’ existing Teal 2 fleet. Delivery is scheduled by August 24, 2026 . The immediate contract value is modest, but the evaluation is strategically important. Successful testing could position Black Widow for broader adoption across active-duty, Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve Security Forces units. The order also builds on Black Widow’s selection for the U.S. Army’s Short Range Reconnaissance program, giving Red Cat another opportunity to establish the platform across a separate military branch. Red Cat also completed a technology-validation event through its SPiDRWORX innovation group, testing integrations across Black Widow and Teal 2 with several industry partners. Notable demonstrations included: Palantir: Vision-based navigation in simulated GPS-denied conditions Safe Pro Group: AI-assisted threat and unexploded-ordnance detection Hoverfly: Tethered-drone communications relay extending network range Vigilare AI: Voice and text commands, visual scene narration and operator alerts Reveal Technology: Imagery, photogrammetry and 3D-mapping workflows

title: U.S. Air Force awards Leidos ISR operations support task order worth up to $717 million
body_text: RESTON, Va. (July 28, 2026) – As global threats become more complex, contested and fast-moving, U.S. airmen need timely intelligence that is trusted and operationally relevant. Leidos (NYSE: LDOS) has been awarded a new task order by the U.S. Air Force's Air Combat Command (ACC) Acquisition Management and Integration Center (AMIC) to continue delivering intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) operations support for ACC. The task order has a total potential value of approximately $717 million if all options are exercised. It includes a one-year base period with four one-year options. Work will be performed at more than 35 locations in the United States and overseas, positioning Leidos personnel alongside U.S. Air Force mission partners at the point of need and reinforcing the company’s role as an embedded partner in day-to-day mission execution. Leidos has supported this mission as the prime contractor since 2019. The new task order extends that partnership at a time when military leaders need accurate, timely information to assess threats and support operations across air, space, cyber and intelligence missions. “Airmen operate in an environment where decisions often depend on the speed, quality and clarity of intelligence,” said Jason McCarthy, Leidos senior vice president, Airborne & Mission Solutions. “Since 2019, our team has worked alongside Air Combat Command to provide mission-focused ISR support, training and analysis. This next phase of work builds on that foundation with the insight and operational expertise needed to help Airmen assess threats, prepare for missions and support operations around the world.” Under the task order, Leidos will provide subject matter expertise, intelligence analysis, threat mitigation, ISR operations support, training, and mission support services for ACC headquarters, subordinate Numbered Air Forces, centers, and wings. This work reflects Leidos' NorthStar 2030 commitment to helping Department of War customers maintain combat-ready forces and defeat evolving global threats. Headquartered at Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Hampton, Virginia, ACC is one of the U.S. Air Force’s major commands and serves as a primary provider of combat air, space, cyber and intelligence capabilities to America’s warfighting commands. ACC AMIC provides acquisition services that support mission-focused capabilities across the command. title: Life of an inference request (vLLM V1): How LLMs are served efficiently at scale
summary: vLLM is an open-source inference engine that serves large language models. We deploy vLLM across GPUs and load open weight models like Llama 4 into it. vLLM sits at the intersection of AI and systems programming, so we thought that diving into its details might interest our readers.
body_text: Life of an inference request (vLLM V1): How LLMs are served efficiently at scale June 27, 2025 · 10 min read Junhao Li Senior Software Engineer Ubicloud is an open source alternative to AWS. We offer managed cloud services that build on top of PostgreSQL, Kubernetes, vLLM, and others. ‍ ‍ vLLM is an open-source inference engine that serves large language models. We deploy multiple vLLM instances across GPUs and load open weight models like Llama 4 into them. We then load balance traffic across vLLM instances, run health checks, and do upgrades. Our customers consume our managed service by sending their prompts to our API endpoints. This endpoint also determines the vLLM instance that serves their prompt. vLLM sits at the intersection of AI and systems programming, so we thought that diving into its details might interest some of our readers. In this blog post, we describe how an inference request travels through vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible API server and core engine. We also provide key code pointers. We assume readers are already familiar with the transformer architecture and large language models. If you're not, we highly recommend this video by OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy. We will focus on the new V1 architecture of vLLM and how it achieves state-of-the-art text generation performance. If you're looking for the V0 behavior or multi-modal inference, please refer to other vLLM documentation. Terminology We use the following terms throughout this blog. These terms also align with what is used in vLLM’s codebase and documentation: Request: An incoming chat completion message from the client, formatted in the OpenAI-compatible format . Sequence: The combined stream of prompt and response tokens associated with a request. Except in special cases, a single request typically corresponds to one sequence. Sequence is sometimes used interchangeably with Request in both the codebase and this blog post. Batching: The process of grouping multiple requests together into a single forward pass through the model to maximize GPU utilization. Prefill: The stage in which the model processes the prompt tokens of a new request. It computes the transformer attention and stores the Key (K) Value (V) tensors of the attention for each token and each layer into the KV cache blocks. Decode: The stage in which the model generates the next output token or the output tensor for intermediate layers repeatedly for ongoing requests. It reuses the stored KV cache of all preceding tokens and computes the Query (Q) tensors based on the most recent token. KV Cache: The GPU memory region used to store the transformer attention keys and values for each token in a request. It is managed globally across all requests and devices in vLLM. KV Block: A fixed-size memory unit in the KV cache that holds keys and values for a fixed number of tokens. KV cache is segmented into blocks to minimize memory reads/writes. High Level Architecture Before diving into the request flow, let’s first take a look at the main components of vLLM V1’s serving architecture: AsyncLLM : An asynchronous wrapper around the core engine. The OpenAI-compatible server uses AsyncLLM to submit requests to and retrieve outputs from the EngineCore asynchronously. It communicates with the EngineCore via AsyncMPClient using asynchronous inter-process communication (IPC). It also handles tokenization and detokenization. EngineCore : The core engine that carries out the inference. It is responsible for scheduling, which means batching and allocating tokens for requests. It also executes the model, processing prompt tokens or generating new ones. It’s the heart of vLLM where most of the logic resides. At the core, there is a busy loop that pulls data from an internal input queue and runs an engine step . An engine step includes the scheduling and execution of one forward pass of the model. The results are first pushed to an internal output queue, and then pushed back to the AsyncLLM and the API server. Two additional background threads manage the asynchronous data transfer between the two internal input/output queues and the AsyncLLM over IPC. Scheduler : A component within the engine that handles how multiple requests are batched. The scheduler maintains queues of requests and decides at each step how many tokens to process for each request. ModelExecutor : A component that coordinates the loading and execution of the model across one or more GPU worker processes. Internally, it uses the ray distributed computing library and launches one worker process per GPU device. ModelRunner : Each GPU worker has a ModelRunner that loads the model and executes the forward passes . The ModelRunner takes requests in batches from the scheduler. It processes these requests through the model on all CUDA cores at the same time. It takes care of assembling input tensors and can use optimizations like CUDA graph capture for repeated executions. KVCacheManager : vLLM’s GPU memory management modules, responsible for managing space for the transformer KV tensors on GPU for all requests. It treats GPU memory as a paging system. KV cache is stored in fixed-size blocks, or pages. This allows for efficient dynamic allocation and avoids needing large contiguous memory reservations. The Scheduler uses the KVCacheManager to allocate these blocks and attaches the block IDs to each request. The ModelRunner then uses these IDs when preparing the execution context. This idea of a paged KV cache was proposed by the vLLM authors in the PagedAttention paper and was the genesis of the vLLM project. Receiving the Request – API Server and Async IPC The journey begins when an HTTP request arrives at the vLLM server (e.g. a POST to /v1/chat/completions). The OpenAI-compatible API server handles the HTTP communication and authentication (via the API key, if configured). This server is often launched by running the vllm serve command defined by vllm/entrypoints/cli/serve.py . After validation, the server invokes the AsyncLLM engine to handle the request. In code, this is done by calling the AsyncLLM engine method generate() . The method is given the prompt and a freshly generated request_id to track this request. When the generate() is called, the AsyncLLM performs tokenization with the model’s tokenizer (often from Hugging Face) to convert text to token IDs. Some multimodal input processing also happens at this stage, but for simplicity, we’ll focus on text prompts here. It then sends the request to the EngineCore via AsyncMPClient using asynchronous IPC calls. Then, a background loop at the EngineCore picks up the request from the IPC channel and places it into an internal input queue for scheduling. Note that the AsyncLLM and EngineCore run in different processes. This bypasses Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL). It allows CPU-intensive tasks, like tokenization and HTTP communication, to run alongside the GPU-intensive task, the model execution. This maximizes overall throughput. Scheduling and Continuous Batching The Scheduler module is central to vLLM’s ability to achieve high throughput. It keeps track of all requests and orchestrates their progress. The scheduler maintains a waiting deque for requests that are ready to be processed (new or resumed ones) and a running list for requests currently in active generation. In each iteration (cycle) of the engine, it first examines the internal input queue and adds new requests into the scheduler’s waiting deque. It then picks a set of requests to advance, looking at the requests from the running list first, and then the requests from the waiting deque. vLLM uses a continuous batching algorithm. This helps maximize GPU utilization by keeping a full workload within a fixed token budget, a.k.a max_num_batched_tokens . It also ensures fairness in request order and limits the batch to just one forward pass of the model. Here’s a continuous batching example: Suppose we have three requests with 3, 5, and 12 prompt tokens, respectively, and a token budget of 10. In a traditional server, these might be handled sequentially or in fixed-size batches. In vLLM, however, the scheduler could decide in one iteration (Step 0) to feed, for example, 3 prompt tokens from R1, 5 from R2, and 2 from R3 in a single forward pass. Note that it only picks two prompt tokens from R3 due to the token budget of 10. In the next iteration (Step 1), it can continue with the remaining 8 prompt tokens from R3. At the same time, it will start generating 1 token each for R1 and R2. They have finished filling their prompt tokens and are now in the decoding phase. Note that during the prefill phase, all prompt tokens from a request can be processed in one batch. This is possible because the query (Q) tensors, calculated from the tokens immediately before them, are available for each prompt token position. In the decoding phase, however, the immediately preceding token must be decoded iteratively, so we can only process one token at a time per request. The scheduler ensures that all requests complete the prefill phase before entering the decoding phase. During the scheduling phase, the KV cache blocks are also determined. The KV Cache Manager groups tokens into fixed-size chunks and either allocates a new KV block or retrieves an existing KV block for each chunk of the tokens. Note that the actual GPU memory allocation occurs during vLLM initialization. The KV Cache Manager determines the block IDs for the KV caches of each request and attaches these IDs to the request, so they can later be used by the ModelRunners when executing the model. Model Execution – Forward Pass on the GPU Once the scheduler has determined which requests to advance, it invokes the ModelRunners via the ray-based ModelExecutor . This executes the model’s forward pass, either processing the prompt tokens or generating new tokens. All tokens from the selected requests are combined into a single large tensor, a.k.a a batch, and are processed layer by layer through the transformer's weight matrices. At each layer, the three attention tensors, Key (K), Value (V), and Query (Q), of each attention head are computed. Then a final attention output tensor for the layer is computed from these tensors. The K and V tensors are stored for future use, and the output tensor becomes the input for the next layer. This is where GPUs come into play, as they are great at large matrix computations. Each tensor includes data from all batched requests. This allows each matrix operation of these requests to be processed on the GPU in parallel using SIMD(T) (single instruction, multiple data, and multiple threads) across all CUDA cores. For requests in the decoding phase, the output tensor from the final transformer layer produces the logits, which represent the predicted probabilities for the next token. vLLM then applies the sampling or decoding strategy . For each sequence, it looks at the logits and either selects the top token (greedy or deterministic) or samples according to the provided parameters, e.g. temperature. This process produces the next token for each batched request. These tokens are placed into an internal output queue, where a background loop picks them up and sends them back to the AsyncLLM via IPC for output processing. This timeline diagram shows a portion of the forward pass for the DeepSeek R1 Distilled Qwen 32B model that we serve. Within the busy loop of the EngineCore, the model's forward method runs. This method calls the forward methods of each transformer layer. Then, the forward method of each layer calls the FlashAttention module. FlashAttention is a highly optimized function for computing transformer attention. It uses the FlashAttention-3 algorithm. This model contains a total of 64 transformer layers and this timeline diagram shows 3 of them at the bottom. The model runner repeats the forward pass through all 64 transformer layers at each engine step. Output Processing – Streaming Tokens Back The AsyncLLM gets the new tokens from the IPC channel. Then, it processes these tokens by detokenizing them and placing them into an internal output queue. The original caller, the AsyncLLM’s generate() function, will then pick them up and pass them back to the API server. In non-streaming mode, the API handler would accumulate tokens internally until the request is finished and then return the final output. In streaming mode, the handler will send each partial output immediately to the client in chunks like data: {...} Conclusion In this blog post, we’ve gone through the entire life of a vLLM inference request. The journey starts with the API server handing the request to the AsyncLLM, which tokenizes and sends requests to the EngineCore. At EngineCore, the scheduler batches requests. The executor works with the ModelRunner to run forward passes through the attention layers on GPUs. Then, tokens are streamed back to clients. Each component plays a distinct role in this lifecycle, and together they allow vLLM to achieve state-of-the-art serving performance. For AI engineers looking to deploy LLMs, we hope understanding this lifecycle helps in tuning and customizing vLLM. For others, we hope this breakdown provides insight into vLLM's inner workings. By doing so, we aim to demystify how large language models are served efficiently and at scale. References https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm https://blog.vllm.ai/2025/01/27/v1-alpha-release.html

title: NBN Outage Work Hubs for Australian Teams
summary: When the NBN Drops, Work Shouldn’t Stop A video pitch freezes mid-sentence. A payroll file refuses to upload. A client call shifts from confident to chaotic in seconds. That is why outage workspaces are becoming […] The post NBN Outage Work Hubs for Australian Teams appeared first on Deskimo .
body_text: When the NBN Drops, Work Shouldn’t Stop A video pitch freezes mid-sentence. A payroll file refuses to upload. A client call shifts from confident to chaotic in seconds. For Australian teams that rely on home broadband, a sudden NBN outage can turn a normal workday into a scramble. That is why outage workspaces are becoming a practical part of remote and hybrid work planning. Whether your team is spread across Sydney suburbs, Melbourne’s inner north, Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide, or regional hubs, backup work locations can protect productivity when home internet fails. Instead of asking employees to tether to unstable mobile data or commute to the head office, companies can prepare a simple “Plan B” that keeps people connected, professional, and focused. Why NBN Outages Hit Hybrid Teams Harder Than They Expect Hybrid work has made Australian organisations more flexible, but it has also shifted more operational risk into employees’ homes. In the office, internet redundancy, meeting rooms, power backup, and IT support are usually managed centrally. At home, a worker may depend on one broadband connection, one router, and one quiet room. When that connection fails, the impact is rarely isolated. One person’s outage can delay a sales demo, interrupt a legal review, stall a finance close, or force a manager to reschedule interviews. For distributed teams, the NBN is no longer just a household utility. It is part of the business infrastructure. The hidden cost of “just work from home” Many teams underestimate the cost of downtime because the interruption looks small on paper. A 90-minute outage may sound manageable, but the knock-on effects can be much larger when the employee is client-facing or working across time zones. Common consequences include: Missed client calls or delayed responses during critical windows Lower meeting quality due to patchy mobile hotspot connections Confidential conversations moved to cafés or public spaces Employees losing time travelling to the office without warning Managers spending time troubleshooting instead of leading Unplanned reimbursements for coworking, mobile data, or transport Australia’s remote work culture has matured quickly, but many policies still assume that home is always available as a reliable workplace. The Australian Bureau of Statistics continues to track working-from-home trends, showing that flexible work is now a mainstream feature of the labour market. Teams can review broader workforce patterns through the ABS working arrangements data to understand how common hybrid arrangements have become. Why mobile hotspots are not a complete backup plan Mobile tethering is useful in a pinch, but it is not enough for every role. A hotspot may handle email and chat, yet struggle with multi-person video calls, large file uploads, virtual desktops, cloud design tools, or CRM-heavy workflows. In apartment buildings, underground locations, storm-affected suburbs, or busy CBD areas, mobile performance can also fluctuate. There are also security and professionalism issues. A finance manager joining a confidential call from a noisy café may be “online,” but not truly work-ready. A recruiter interviewing candidates from a public table may be visible and audible to strangers. That is where outage workspaces provide a more dependable alternative: business-grade internet, proper seating, quiet areas, and meeting facilities when home connectivity fails. How Outage Workspaces Fit Into an Australian Business Continuity Plan Business continuity planning often focuses on cyber incidents, power failures, extreme weather, and office access. Yet for hybrid teams, a home internet outage can be just as disruptive to daily operations. A practical continuity plan should include clear instructions for where employees can work if their home connection is unavailable. Outage workspaces are not about replacing the home office. They are about giving employees a fast, approved fallback option. When the NBN drops, staff should not need to ask five people for permission, search online for a nearby café, or guess whether an expense will be reimbursed. What makes a workspace suitable during an outage? Not every alternate location is appropriate. A good outage workspace should support productive work immediately, with minimal setup time and predictable quality. Look for these essentials: Reliable high-speed internet that can support video calls and cloud tools Comfortable desks and ergonomic seating for focused work Quiet areas or call rooms for confidential conversations Power outlets and backup power where possible Convenient locations near residential suburbs, transit routes, and client districts Simple access without long contracts or manual invoicing Clear usage reporting for HR, finance, and operations teams For teams with employees in multiple cities, consistency matters. A worker in Parramatta, South Yarra, Fortitude Valley, Subiaco, or Canberra’s inner south should be able to follow the same process: check availability, book a spot, and keep working. Build outage response around roles, not seniority A common mistake is to reserve backup work options only for executives. In reality, the people most affected by outages may be customer support agents, recruiters, account managers, finance staff, engineers, consultants, and project coordinators. Consider ranking roles by outage sensitivity: Client-critical roles: sales, account management, consulting, legal, advisory, and customer success Operations-critical roles: finance, payroll, scheduling, compliance, and IT support Collaboration-heavy roles: product teams, designers, marketers, recruiters, and managers Deep-work roles: analysts, developers, writers, and researchers who may need stable access to cloud tools This approach helps companies decide who needs instant access to outage workspaces, who can wait a few hours, and who can continue asynchronously. It also avoids the perception that workspace access is a perk rather than a resilience tool. Choosing the Right Work Hubs Before the Next Outage The best time to choose backup work locations is before an outage occurs. Once the connection is already down, employees are under pressure, meetings are approaching, and good decision-making becomes harder. A pre-approved hub network gives everyone a clear path. Australian teams should think beyond CBD coworking. The ideal solution may include neighbourhood workspaces close to where employees live, client-adjacent hubs near meeting locations, and quiet rooms for secure calls. This is especially important in cities where commuting from outer suburbs to a central office can take an hour or more each way. Map employee locations and common outage scenarios Start with a simple location audit. You do not need exact home addresses to plan effectively. Postcode-level data is often enough to identify clusters of employees who would benefit from nearby backup locations. Ask these practical questions: Which suburbs have the highest concentration of hybrid employees? Which roles require reliable video calls every day? Which employees live far from the main office? Which teams work with international clients outside standard Australian business hours? Which locations are most vulnerable to storm disruption, local infrastructure works, or mobile congestion? Employees can check current network issues through the NBN network status page , but a status page alone does not solve the problem. Teams still need a practical place to go when work cannot wait. Prioritise secure calls and professional environments During an outage, the temptation is to find the nearest place with Wi-Fi. That may be a café, library, shopping centre, or hotel lobby. These options can work for light admin, but they are risky for confidential or high-stakes work. Privacy matters for HR conversations, board updates, contract negotiations, medical-adjacent services, legal discussions, financial reviews, and enterprise sales. If employees are expected to handle sensitive information, they need access to spaces designed for professional calls. For deeper guidance on this topic, see secure call pods for Australian hybrid teams . Security is also about behaviour. Provide employees with a short checklist for outage days: Use company-approved VPN and multi-factor authentication Avoid discussing confidential matters in open public areas Use headphones for calls Lock screens when stepping away Confirm that any booked room is suitable for sensitive discussions Practical Playbook: Setting Up Outage Workspaces for Your Team A useful outage plan should be simple enough for employees to follow under pressure. If it requires multiple approvals, manual forms, or manager-by-manager discretion, it will fail when people need it most. Treat outage workspaces like a standard operating procedure, not an ad hoc benefit. The goal is to create a repeatable path from “my NBN is down” to “I am working productively from a suitable nearby hub.” Step 1: Define when employees should use a backup workspace Start by setting clear triggers. This prevents confusion and gives managers confidence that workspace use is legitimate. Examples of reasonable triggers include: Home internet is unavailable for more than 30 minutes during core working hours Mobile hotspot speed is not sufficient for scheduled meetings The employee has a client presentation, interview, or deadline within the next three hours The outage affects a role that is part of payroll, customer support, incident response, or revenue operations The employee cannot work securely from a public venue Be specific, but avoid making the policy overly rigid. A senior consultant preparing for a client workshop may need a workspace immediately, while another employee can shift to offline work for an hour. Step 2: Set budgets, approvals, and reporting Finance teams often worry that flexible workspace access will create uncontrolled spending. That risk is real if employees are left to book whatever they find and expense it later. A better approach is to set clear budgets and use platforms that provide centralised reporting. This is where companies should also watch for hidden costs. When employees pay for cafés, coworking day passes, hotel lounges, or transport out of pocket, workspace spend becomes fragmented and hard to measure. The issue is similar to the broader challenge of shadow workspace spend in hybrid teams , where untracked expenses can quietly grow across departments. A clean policy should answer: Who is eligible to book an outage workspace? What is the daily or monthly usage limit? Can employees book meeting rooms or only desks? Who approves exceptions? How will usage be reported to HR, operations, and finance? For many Australian businesses, the answer is not a large fixed office footprint. It is controlled access to flexible work hubs that employees use only when needed. Step 3: Communicate the plan before a disruption A policy is only useful if employees know it exists. Share the outage process during onboarding, hybrid work refreshers, manager training, and business continuity reviews. Keep the instructions short and easy to find. A simple internal message could say: “If your home NBN connection is down and you have time-sensitive work, check the network status, notify your manager, and book an approved workspace near you. Use a private room for confidential calls and record the reason as ‘connectivity outage’.” Managers should model the behaviour too. If leaders treat backup workspaces as a normal productivity tool, employees are less likely to feel guilty about using them. Local Factors Australian Teams Should Consider Australia’s geography makes workspace resilience different from many other markets. Major cities are spread out, suburban commuting can be time-consuming, and weather events can affect both connectivity and transport. A backup plan that works in Singapore or central London may not fit Western Sydney, outer Melbourne, regional Queensland, or Perth’s northern corridor. That is why outage workspaces should be planned around real travel patterns, not just office addresses. CBD backup is useful, but neighbourhood access is better A central office can be a backup option, but it is not always the fastest one. If an employee in Penrith, Geelong, Joondalup, or Logan loses internet, sending them to a CBD office may cost half a day in travel and fatigue. A closer workspace can preserve both productivity and wellbeing. Near-home and near-client work hubs are especially valuable when employees have meetings across the city. Instead of returning home between appointments or travelling back to the head office, they can use professional spaces close to where work is happening. This also connects with a broader productivity strategy: near-client workspaces that cut dead time . For business travellers, the same principle applies. A consultant arriving in Melbourne for a workshop or a founder visiting Sydney investors should not depend entirely on hotel Wi-Fi. A reliable workspace near the meeting location can keep the day on track. Plan for weather, power, and infrastructure disruption NBN interruptions are not the only risk. Severe storms, flooding, heatwaves, construction works, and power disruptions can affect home-based work. The Bureau of Meteorology provides regular updates and warnings through Australia’s official weather service , which can help operations teams anticipate disruption in affected regions. Some outage events are local and brief. Others are part of broader infrastructure stress. Teams should identify which work hubs offer not only strong internet, but also dependable power and comfortable conditions. Lessons from other Asia-Pacific markets can be useful here, particularly in cities where backup power is a daily business concern. For example, Deskimo’s guide to power backup workspaces for Jakarta teams offers practical thinking that Australian companies can adapt for storm-prone or disruption-sensitive regions. It is also worth creating a hierarchy of fallback options: First option: approved nearby workspace with reliable internet and call facilities Second option: company office or satellite office, if travel time is reasonable Third option: mobile hotspot for low-sensitivity tasks Last resort: public venue for non-confidential work only Making Outage Workspaces Part of a Better Hybrid Work Culture Backup work hubs are not just an IT fix. They are a sign of a mature hybrid culture. When companies acknowledge that home work has real infrastructure limits, they can support employees without forcing everyone back into a fixed office model. The strongest policies balance flexibility, trust, and accountability. Employees get practical options when something goes wrong. Managers get continuity. Finance gets visibility. Clients get a smoother experience. Measure outcomes, not just usage After introducing outage workspaces, track whether the policy is improving the employee and business experience. Usage data is helpful, but it should not be the only metric. Consider reviewing: Number of outage-related workspace bookings by city or suburb Teams or roles with the highest need for backup locations Client meetings saved from cancellation Employee feedback on commute time and workspace quality Reduction in unplanned reimbursements Manager satisfaction with continuity during disruptions This data can help HR and operations teams refine eligibility, budgets, and location coverage. It can also support broader decisions about office footprint, hybrid work expectations, and employee experience. Keep the policy human Connectivity failures are stressful. Employees may already be dealing with children at home, transport delays, bad weather, or urgent deadlines. A good outage policy should reduce anxiety, not add more admin. Use plain language. Make booking easy. Trust employees to make reasonable decisions. Provide guidance for secure work, but avoid turning every outage into a compliance maze. The most effective message is simple: “If your connection fails, you have somewhere professional to go.” That clarity is valuable for remote workers, entrepreneurs, freelancers, and corporate teams alike. Keep Australian Teams Connected When the Unexpected Happens NBN outages are a reality of modern work, but they do not have to derail the day. With the right plan, Australian teams can move from reactive scrambling to calm continuity. The key is to identify suitable outage workspaces in advance, define when they should be used, protect confidential work, and keep spending visible. For hybrid organisations, this is a practical way to strengthen resilience without abandoning flexibility. For freelancers and business travellers, it offers a professional fallback when home, hotel, or mobile internet is not enough. And for managers, it keeps people productive without forcing unnecessary commutes to a central office. title: The Sub Shop That Solved the Growth Trap.
summary: Jersey Mike's became the first new brand to top the ACSI's quick-service rankings in more than a decade, all while adding over 1,000 restaurants. Here's how the sandwich chain kept growth from eroding its operations.
body_text: Jersey Mike’s Subs has had a remarkable few years. The sandwich chain recently became the first new restaurant to top the American Customer Satisfaction Index’s quick-service rankings in more than a decade, earning a score of 84/100 based on more than 16,000 customer surveys. While many growing restaurant brands eventually see operational performance flatten, or even decline, Jersey Mike’s has continued improving while adding more than 1,000 net new restaurants over the past four years. Its average unit volumes have continued climbing. Same-store sales have now grown for 20 consecutive years. Customer satisfaction has improved enough to become America’s highest-rated QSR. Preventing operational complexity from outpacing operational consistency like that is an unusually difficult thing to pull off. The Growth Trap Growth doesn’t usually fail all at once — it slowly becomes harder to manage. Restaurant leaders spend a lot of time talking about growth, but growth creates its own operational challenges. Every additional restaurant means more managers, employees, digital orders, variability, and more opportunities for execution to become inconsistent. Eventually, many brands reach a point where adding restaurants becomes easier than maintaining the standards that made them successful in the first place. Jersey Mike’s appears to have avoided that trap. Since 2006, the company has increased average unit volume every single year, growing from roughly $423,000 to $1.36 million in 2025. Systemwide sales also increased from $3.7 billion in 2024 to $4.2 billion in 2025. For a brand that now operates more than 3,200 restaurants, that’s sustained operational performance. About a year ago, Jersey Mike’s leadership reportedly noticed something concerning. Small operational warning signs were beginning to appear: cleanliness wasn’t as consistent, some restaurants were shutting grills down early. Nothing catastrophic, but enough to recognize that growth was beginning to put pressure on execution. Instead of continuing business as usual, the company reportedly paused parts of its national expansion, refunded franchise fees, and shifted its attention back toward training before accelerating growth again. That’s a decision that rarely makes headlines. It probably should. The willingness to slow expansion in order to protect operational standards may be one of the biggest reasons the company has been able to continue growing without sacrificing customer experience. The takeaway: growth doesn’t create great operations. Great operations make sustainable growth possible. Building Capacity Before Adding Complexity The company invested in existing restaurants — not just new ones. Another detail that stands out is where Jersey Mike’s invested. Digital ordering has grown from roughly 15% of sales before the pandemic to around 40% today. Rather than simply opening more restaurants to absorb that demand, the company invested inside existing ones: dedicated digital make lines, updated counters, store remodels designed specifically to improve throughput. In one group of remodeled Los Angeles restaurants, those investments reportedly helped drive a 30% increase in sales, compared to roughly 15% at locations that hadn’t yet been updated. It’s an important reminder that scaling isn’t always about building more capacity, sometimes it’s about making the capacity you already have work better. Growing With People Who Already Know the System Expansion becomes easier when experience scales alongside it. One of the most overlooked parts of this growth story isn’t how many restaurants it has opened, it’s who has been opening them. Roughly 85% of the company’s recent expansion has come from existing franchisees. At the same time, Jersey Mike’s has continued investing in its internal Coach Program, helping successful managers and assistant managers become franchise owners themselves. That’s a different approach than simply recruiting as many new operators as possible. As restaurant systems grow, maintaining consistency becomes increasingly difficult. Expanding with people who already understand the brand’s standards, culture, and operating model reduces that learning curve and helps preserve the consistency that customers expect. It’s a reminder that scaling isn’t just about adding restaurants. It’s about scaling experience, operational knowledge, and leadership alongside them. “One of the biggest mistakes growing brands make is assuming every new location is a real estate decision. In reality, it’s a people decision. The operators you choose to grow with often determine whether expansion strengthens the system — or stretches it too thin.” — Rob Green, VP of Revenue, Berry AI
